rv.q: ‘The Antipodes’ – which has its UK premiere in a production co-directed by Baker herself and designer Chloe Lamford – is utterly, gloriously out there and will doubtless horrify some people.

What’s clever about the play (jointly directed by Baker and Lamford) is that it deepens and darkens the themes while remaining grounded and funny, and it’s peppered with beautifully detailed performances.
But for a night round a crazy campfire, I absolutely loved it.
Line by line, there aren’t many other playwrights who provide such consistent pleasure.
Its disquieting mood lingers long, long after its abrupt snap ending.
Aficionados of the characteristic Baker rhythm – uptight fretful lassitude, which occasionally breaks into laugh-out-loud hilarity – will not be disappointed.
Baker’s play falls apart only when the characters are left to their own devices and when it seeks to make general statements.
However, the absence of a conventional narrative makes it a gruelling ride for the unconverted.
Baker’s latest effort, The Antipodes, is lifeless, pseudish, repetitive and, in a new production at the National Theatre, not even that well staged.
Hours after the performance had ended, I found I was still thinking of the play and its themes, pulling at threads, thrilled by its rich ambition.
Annie Baker is a contemplative and challenging playwright who gives viewers an opportunity to explore the minutiae of life in great detail.
I was as gripped as I was frequently perplexed.
Characters with no interest in the dramatic outcome of the story in which they feature are incapable of engaging an audience.
This is an ineffectual production of a limp idea.
It’s still Baker though who pushes dangerously at just what theatre is.
To some, it is sophisticated, but to me, it makes me wonder if there is any substance, point or purpose to the more realistic aspects of the show.
On the surface The Antipodes seems to be a satire on corporate brainstorming, but why does Sandy slowly retreat from the group and quite what is wrong with his wife Rachel?
It’s hard work to sit through, though.

cn.t: Critics are sharply divided on Baker's surreal corporate satire—some find it wickedly clever and hypnotic, others maddeningly repetitive. Conleth Hill's performance earns praise, but patience is required.
